newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU set to tighten food safety rules.
newsitem.headline: EU set to tighten food safety rules.

text.p: The European Union's executive, under pressure from Britain and the European Parliament, is ready to introduce stricter rules to protect consumers from mad cow disease if the 15-nation bloc's farm ministers fail to act on Tuesday.

A European Commission spokesman said that the executive would implement a proposal to remove risky animal tissue such as brains and spinal cords from human and animal food, cosmetics and medicine if Tuesday's ministerial meeting proved inconclusive.
The proposal can either be adopted by a weighted majority at the meeting or rejected by a simple majority of eight votes.
"We want to have this proposal put through one way or another, ideally through the Council, failing that through the Commission," the spokesman said.
Britain, which already applies the measure, has warned that if the proposal isn't adopted this week it will ensure that beef imports comply with rigorous British food safety standards.

The European Parliament has threatened to sack the EU's 20 commissioners unless they take stronger action by November to protect public health and eradicate the fatal cattle brain disease, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE).
Last week, the EU's Standing Veterinary Committee of senior member state officials narrowly rejected the proposal.

EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler regretted the decision, saying it was unacceptable, in view of public concern about BSE, that some member states refuse to apply necessary precautions to protect human and animal health.
European Commission officials said ministers, sensitive to public opinion, could vote differently from veterinary experts.
"Otherwise they risk being accused of putting economics above human health," said the Commission spokesman.
Last December, only Britain, Ireland, France, Sweden and Luxembourg supported a similar proposal to remove the risky animal parts.
Other countries argued that it was an unnecessary expense as they were free of BSE and scrapie, a similar brain wasting disease in sheep.
But EU veterinary inspections have revealed widespread shortcomings, prompting the Commission last month to take legal action against 10 countries.

"No country can say with 100 percent certainty that they don't have BSE or scrapie," the spokesman said, adding that BSE came from scrapie and that no country has been officially declared to be "scrapie free."
In the single EU market, the same rules must apply in all member states irrespective of the level of disease, he said, adding that removal of the risky tissue was not costly.

The Netherlands, where two cases of BSE have been reported, and Spain last week swung round to support the Commission's proposal to remove the brain, eyes, tonsils and spinal cord of slaughtered cattle, sheep and goats over 12 months of age which would otherwise enter the food chain.
EU sources said that on Tuesday Portugal or Belgium could also switch and either vote for the proposal or abstain, thus enabling the Commission to act.
